doc.title: Doug Carn interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 24, 2023

title: Retirement, age and coaching a protege
summary: He recalls Jay McShann at Kansas City, doubts he will stop playing, and speaks of grandchildren and coaching.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Being honored: NEA Jazz Masters and other awards

blocks.x: I was five years old and he was playing and I’m there, not on the dais but in the broader distinguished people for what it was and I looked him tiptoeing out to the piano smiling, you know balancing on air with his two hands. So I told the boy sitting next to me, I said, “Man when I get so old that I can’t hardly walk and hold my water and stuff, I ain’t going to keep playing and I’m going to quit. I’m going to retire you know. I ain’t going to play no more. And there was another old man, he had to be about 90 himself, he said, “If they give you fifty thousand dollars you will.”
Oh that’s a good way to wrap up, and I’m going to look for fifty grand to send your way.
The grandchildren need it. I’ve got three great grands man.

And I can’t go and see them, they’re going to have to come and see me you know. Every now and then I get under the weather. I’m under the weather now you know. But I can play you know. But I don’t want to be having to creep to the piano then get carried away from the piano on a stretcher you know. You know I’ll play for a while or if anything I

will get a protégé and get him to play and sit on the sidelines and coach him along you know, and root for him you know. It’s just like being a football coach or a boxing coach or a golf coach you know, you can’t really play good no more, but you’ve got knowledge so you can participate in some way. But when you get so old they’re not getting out — they used to get out there and try to quarterback you know.
